## Dataset: Calibration data for empirical mortality models of 18 European tree species

The dataset comprises - 90 000 records from inventories in 54 strict forest reserves in &#91;Switzerland&#93;&#40;https://www.wsl.ch/de/wald/biodiversitaet-naturschutz-urwald/naturwaldreservate.html&#41; and &#91;Lower Saxony / Germany&#93;&#40;http://naturwaelder.de/&#41; along a considerable environmental gradient. It was used to develop parsimonious, species-specific mortality models for 18 European tree species based on tree size and growth as well as additional covariates on stand structure and climate. <br> Inventory data<br>Measurements had been conducted repeatedly on up to 14 permanent plots per reserve for up to 60 years with re-measurement intervals of 4 - 27 years. The permanent plots vary in size between 0.03 and 3.47 ha. The inventories provide diameter measurements at breast height &#40;DBH&#41; and information on the species and status &#40;alive or dead&#41; of trees with DBH ≥ 4 cm for Switzerland and ≥ 7 cm for Germany. <br> Data selection<br>We excluded three permanent plots where at least 80 % of the trees died during an interval of 10 years, and mortality could be clearly assigned to a disturbance agent. Mortality in the remaining stands was rather low, with a mean annual mortality rate of 1.5 % and strong variation between plots from 0 to 6.5 % &#40;assessed for trees of all species with DBH ≥ 7 cm&#41;.<br>We only used data from permanent plots with at least 20 trees per species to obtain reliable plot-level mortality rates even for species with low mortality rates &#40;about 5 % during 10 years&#41;, and selected tree species occurring on at least 10 plots to cover sufficient ecological gradients. This led to a dataset of 197 permanent plots and 18 tree or shrub species: &#95;Abies alba&#95; Mill., &#95;Acer campestre&#95; L., &#95;Acer pseudoplatanus&#95; L., &#95;Alnus incana&#95; Moench., &#95;Betula pendula&#95; Roth, &#95;Carpinus betulus&#95; L., &#95;Cornus mas&#95; L., &#95;Corylus avellana&#95; L., &#95;Fagus sylvatica&#95; L., &#95;Fraxinus excelsior&#95; L., &#95;Picea abies&#95; &#40;L.&#41; Karst, &#95;Pinus mugo&#95; Turra, &#95;Pinus sylvestris&#95; L., &#95;Quercus pubescens&#95; Willd., &#95;Quercus&#95; spp. &#40;&#95;Q. petraea&#95; Liebl. and &#95;Q. robur&#95; L.; not properly differentiated in the Swiss inventories&#41;, &#95;Sorbus aria&#95; Crantz, &#95;Tilia cordata&#95; Mill. and &#95;Ulmus glabra&#95; Huds.. <br> Predictors of tree mortality<br>We considered tree size and growth as key indicators for mortality risk. Radial stem growth between the first and second inventory and DBH at the second inventory were used to predict tree status &#40;alive or dead&#41; at the third inventory. To this end, the annual relative basal area increment &#40;relBAI&#41; was calculated as the compound annual growth rate of the trees basal area. Additional covariates on stand structure and climate comprise mean annual precipitation sum &#40;P&#41;, mean annual air temperature &#40;mT&#41;, the mean and the interquartile range of DBH &#40;mDBH, iqrDBH&#41;, basal area &#40;BA&#41; and the number of trees &#40;N&#41; per hectare. <br> Further information<br>For further information, refer to Hülsmann &#95;et al&#95;. &#40;in press&#41; How to kill a tree – Empirical mortality models for eighteen species and their performance in a dynamic forest model. &#95;Ecological Applications&#95;.

[View this dataset in the data catalogue](https://opendata.swiss/de/dataset/calibration-data-for-empirical-mortality-models-of-18-european-tree-species)

## Load packages

This template targets tidyverse (2.x) and skimr (2.x) with R 4.1 or newer for the native `|>` pipe; package versions are not pinned. Install missing packages once with `install.packages(c("tidyverse", "skimr"))`.

```{r setup, message=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(skimr)
theme_set(theme_minimal())

USER_AGENT <- "OpendataSwiss-StarterCode-R/1.0"
HTTP_TIMEOUT <- 30

get_dataset <- function(url, delim = NULL, drop_empty_unnamed = TRUE, ...) {
  if (grepl("^https?://", url)) {
    local_file <- tempfile()
    on.exit(unlink(local_file), add = TRUE)
    old_options <- options(timeout = HTTP_TIMEOUT)
    on.exit(options(old_options), add = TRUE)
    status <- download.file(url, local_file, method = "libcurl", mode = "wb",
                            quiet = TRUE, headers = c("User-Agent" = USER_AGENT))
    if (status != 0) stop("Resource download failed")
    url <- local_file
  }
  data <- read_delim(url, delim = delim, show_col_types = FALSE, ...)
  stop_for_problems(data)
  if (drop_empty_unnamed && nrow(data) > 0) {
    # Blank CSV headers (often from trailing separators) become "...n".
    unnamed <- grepl("^\\.\\.\\.[0-9]+$", names(data))
    empty_unnamed <- unnamed & map_lgl(data, ~ all(is.na(.x)))
    if (any(empty_unnamed)) {
      message("Removed empty unnamed columns: ", paste(names(data)[empty_unnamed], collapse = ", "))
      data <- data[, !empty_unnamed, drop = FALSE]
    }
  }
  data
}
```

## Load data

Selected resource: **8c81af92-f8e7-4c94-976a-21ee59a3419f** (CSV). This notebook loads only this resource.

For CSV, the delimiter and column types are guessed. Check the preview and metadata; set `delim`, `col_types`, `na`, or `locale` in `get_dataset(...)` when needed (for example, read identifiers with leading zeros as character columns). Parsing problems stop the import so they can be addressed.

Fully empty columns named `...n` are removed on import. Named empty columns and unnamed columns containing values are kept. Use `drop_empty_unnamed = FALSE` to retain every column, including intentionally named `...n` fields.

```{r load-data}

```

## Missing values

```{r missing-values}
missing <- tibble(
  column = names(df),
  missing = map_int(df, ~ sum(is.na(.x))),
  missing_pct = map_dbl(df, ~ mean(is.na(.x)) * 100)
) |>
  arrange(desc(missing_pct))
missing

# Show up to 20 columns with missing values; percentages use all rows.
missing_plot <- missing |> filter(missing > 0) |> slice_head(n = 20)
if (nrow(missing_plot) > 0) {
  ggplot(missing_plot, aes(x = missing_pct, y = reorder(column, missing_pct))) +
    geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
    scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 100)) +
    labs(x = "Missing values (%)", y = NULL, title = "Missingness by column")
} else {
  message("No missing values to plot (or the dataset has no rows).")
}
```

## Summary and distributions

`skim()` reports completeness and type-specific summaries. Inspect units before interpreting numeric codes as measurements.

```{r summary}
if (nrow(df) > 0 && ncol(df) > 0) {
  skim(df)
} else {
  message("No data to summarize.")
}
```

```{r histograms}
# Plot up to four numeric columns, excluding non-finite values only from plots.
numeric_names <- names(select(df, where(is.numeric))) |> head(4)
for (column in numeric_names) {
  values <- df[[column]]
  values <- values[is.finite(values)]
  if (length(values) > 0) {
    plot <- ggplot(tibble(value = values), aes(x = value)) +
      geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "steelblue", colour = "white") +
      labs(title = column, x = column, y = "Count")
    print(plot)
  }
}
```

```{r category-counts}
# Top 10 values for up to three categorical columns, including missing values.
categorical_names <- df |>
  select(where(~ is.character(.x) || is.factor(.x) || is.logical(.x))) |>
  names() |>
  head(3)
for (column in categorical_names) {
  cat(column, "\n")
  df |> count(.data[[column]], sort = TRUE) |> head(10) |> print()
}
```
